analysis.one_liner: Doubles federal cigarette taxes, raises taxes on other tobacco products, and taxes vaping nicotine for the first time.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have doubled the federal cigarette tax from $50.33 to $100.66 per thousand and imposed the first federal tax on vaping nicotine, died in the House Ways and Means Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have roughly doubled the federal excise tax on cigarettes and sharply raised taxes on cigars, pipe tobacco, smokeless tobacco, and roll-your-own tobacco, bringing them to the same per-pound rate as cigarettes. It would also have created the first federal tax on the nicotine used in vaping, while exempting FDA-approved quit-smoking products like nicotine gum and patches. The goal was to close loopholes that let smokers avoid taxes by switching to cheaper tobacco products, and to discourage smoking and vaping. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The federal Treasury, through roughly doubled cigarette tax revenue and new revenue from other tobacco products and vaping nicotine [S3]. Public health broadly, since tobacco taxes are one of the most effective tools for reducing smoking, and lower-income communities suffer the most tobacco-related disease. People who quit or never start smoking gain the most. Makers of FDA-approved nicotine replacement therapies (gum, patches, lozenges) also gain relatively, because the bill explicitly exempts their products from the new nicotine tax [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal Treasury and public health; quitters gain most

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the federal cigarette excise tax from $50.33 to $100.66 per thousand cigarettes (and $105.69 to $211.38 for large cigarettes), a price increase that research consistently shows reduces smoking, especially among young people.

Ends tax loopholes that let smokers avoid taxes by switching products: pipe tobacco was taxed at $2.8311 per pound while roll-your-own tobacco was taxed at $24.78 per pound, so the bill sets both at $49.56, and raises smokeless tobacco from $1.51 to $26.84 per pound.
Imposes the first federal excise tax on nicotine used in vaping, at the same per-nicotine rate as cigarettes, closing a gap that made vaping cheaper than smoking for the same nicotine dose.
Exempts FDA-approved smoking-cessation drugs and combination products from the nicotine tax, so quitting aids like gum and patches would not get more expensive.

Indexes all tobacco tax rates to inflation so they stop eroding in real terms every year, and imposes a floor stocks tax on tobacco inventory held when the rates rise so stockpilers cannot dodge the increase.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers and vapers, who would pay roughly twice as much federal tax per pack and a new tax on vaping nicotine; tobacco taxes are regressive, falling hardest on lower-income users. Tobacco manufacturers and vape companies bear the tax and new permit and bond requirements, and retailers pay a floor stocks tax on inventory they hold on the effective date [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Smokers, vapers, and tobacco and vape companies

drawbacks.text: Tobacco taxes are regressive: because smoking is concentrated among lower-income people, doubling the cigarette tax would have taken the largest share of its revenue from working-class smokers rather than from tobacco company profits.

Taxing vaping nicotine at the same rate as cigarettes could push vapers back to cigarettes; many public health researchers argue vaping is substantially less harmful than smoking, so equalizing the rates removes a financial incentive to switch.

The jump for some products was extreme: the pipe tobacco rate would have gone from about $2.83 per pound to $49.56, roughly a seventeenfold increase, which would impose abrupt and large cost increases on a legal product's users.
The floor stocks tax would force retailers and distributors to pay the tax difference on all inventory held the day rates rose, within 120 days, a cash burden that falls hardest on small shops.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is real: doubling cigarette taxes and closing the loopholes that let people switch to cheaper tobacco products would reduce smoking and save lives, and the exemption for FDA-approved quitting aids is a thoughtful design feature. But the costs are also real and fall mostly on lower-income people who smoke or vape, not on tobacco company shareholders alone, since excise taxes are passed through to prices. The vaping tax is the weakest part, because it treats a less harmful alternative to cigarettes the same as cigarettes. On balance a defensible public health measure with a genuinely regressive price tag.

outcome.mechanism: The House Ways and Means Committee never took the bill up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced the Tobacco Tax Equity Act of 2023 on September 26, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over excise taxes.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, a fellow Democrat.
No further action of any kind was taken: no hearing, no markup, no vote. The bill sat in committee until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, at which point it died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers, vaping companies, and retailers came out ahead, keeping the current low rates and the loopholes the bill would have closed; cigarette and cigar smokers also kept today's prices. Public health advocates, who wanted higher tobacco taxes, got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco and vaping companies; users' prices unchanged

for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Jason Smith)

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no split can be measured; the Democratic sponsor found one Democratic cosponsor, and the bill died in the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee.

industries.note: The bill would have doubled cigarette tax rates, raised smokeless and pipe tobacco rates by roughly 10 to 17 times, ended the favorable per-unit cap on large cigars, and taxed already-manufactured inventory through a floor stocks tax. It also would have closed the loopholes that let price-sensitive smokers migrate to lightly taxed products, protecting the industry's volume.

The bill would impose the first federal excise tax on nicotine for vaping, at the cigarette-equivalent rate per 1,810 milligrams of nicotine, and would treat anyone who extracts, concentrates, or synthesizes nicotine as a tobacco manufacturer subject to permits and bonds. The bill's death leaves vaping nicotine untaxed at the federal level.

A floor stocks tax would have required anyone holding tobacco inventory when rates rose to pay the difference within 120 days, with only a $500 credit, a cash squeeze on small shops; higher prices would also likely cut sales volume.

industries.industry: Nicotine replacement therapy makers (gum, patches, lozenges)
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts nicotine used in FDA-approved drugs from the new nicotine tax, giving approved quitting aids a growing price advantage over taxed cigarettes and vapes.
